items.excerpt:
Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember . Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as:
[...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.
For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40.
The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others:
But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem.
For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis.
And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models:
The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement:
It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.
(That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!)
Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response.
Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too:
The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember.
This is a link post by Simon Willison, posted on 10th November 2026 .

items.excerpt:
November 9, 2026 — Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 arrive on Anthropic’s IPO roadshow day. How much thinking is worth paying for?
On Friday, we asked Jamin Ball what comes next for Anthropic’s IPO . On Monday the roadshow started and Anthropic shipped the long-anticipated next-version of Claude Fable and Mythos . Of course, it is the new top model in the world, taking back Opus 5.5’s #1 spot from Gemini 4 Carbon which had its brief moment in the sun (10 days).
Fable comes with a 20% per token price cut… but is more token hungry, as both SemiAnalysis GDPx and Artificial Analysis agree:
Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 costs $8 and $40 . Yet on GDPx, a benchmark of professional tasks, SemiAnalysis paid $88.15 per task, up from $67.16 . The run logs give a clue. Where Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 would try about 20 test cases, 5.2 sometimes wrote hundreds or thousands and spun up subagents to check its work independently. All that checking helped Fable take first place at 16.4% . You pay for the checks either way.
Which effort setting should you put in production? On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable at High matched Opus 5.5 at Max for about half the cost per task… but don’t talk about Fable at Max.

items.excerpt:
Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked.
If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own:
You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you.
The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it.
— Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation
This is a quotation collected by Simon Willison, posted on 10th November 2026 .

items.title: Import Cargo Still Strong as Peak Season Winds Down
items.description: "New tariffs introduced in the second quarter prompted a renewed surge in imports beginning in May that continued through mid-October," said Ben Hackett.
items.excerpt:
Following an extended peak season that has kept docks busy since the spring, import volume at the nation’s major container ports is expected to taper off for the remainder of the year, according to the Global Port Tracker report released on November 9 by the National Retail Federation and Hackett Associate s. “U.S. ports have seen high volume levels throughout this year’s longer-than-usual peak season and numbers are still strong even as the season winds down,” NRF vice president for Supply Chain and Customs Policy Jonathan Gold said in a statement.
“Unfortunately, these volumes have led to backups at some ports, particularly on the West Coast where cargo has sat for extended periods waiting to be transferred to rail cars. We’ve also seen the threat of a strike at the nation’s largest port complex in recent days. Nonetheless, most holiday merchandise is already here, and retailers are working closely with their supply chain partners to ensure that the supply of holiday gifts continues to flow smoothly.”
A strike was avoided at the beginning of the month when International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26, which represents watchmen at a number of container terminals at the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, reached a short-term contract extension with the Pacific Maritime Association.
The contract has now been extended three times for a few days at a time, most recently through Nov. 20, with no long-term agreement in place following the expiration of the previous contract in July 2025. Hackett Associates Founder Ben Hackett said this year’s months-long peak season was an offshoot of an extended season in 2025, when a series of tariff increases led retailers to bring in merchandise before the tariffs could take effect. “At the start of 2026, that surge appeared to have ended after the Supreme Court struck down high ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs. Expectations of another extended peak season consequently faded,” Hackett said. “However, new tariffs introduced in the second quarter prompted a renewed surge in imports beginning in May that continued through mid-October. Consumer spending supported this influx, with households continuing to buy despite rising inflation.” U.S. ports covered by Global Port Tracker handled 2.37 million TEUs in September, the latest month for which final numbers are available. items.title: Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account
items.excerpt:
You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace .
Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs , deploying models with Inference Endpoints , calling thousands of models through Inference Providers , or hosting demos on GPU Spaces .
If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:
If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.
Go to the Hugging Face Hub listing on the Google Cloud Marketplace, select the Google Cloud project you want to use, and click on "Subscribe".
You are now on the subscription page. Select the billing account to be charged, review and accept the terms, then click "Subscribe".
Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.
You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.
You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.
Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

items.title: Decision Models in Hugging Face
items.excerpt:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.
Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:
"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."
The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.
We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.
But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text ?
This is the key idea behind decision models .
A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.
TypeSafe AI introduced Jev , describing it as a System One model . The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).
The community has converged to the term decision model , because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". ( A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models )
For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:
We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.
However, there are a few problems with this approach.
Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.
Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

items.excerpt:
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven’t unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn’t want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.
Here’s what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:
You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners—I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.
The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn’t work particularly well, so I added a “Rough mode” where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.
Once that’s set up, the devices all listen for the beep!
I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room—displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.
Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the “Sounds located” log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click “This is the mystery beep” to mark them as such.
Once you’ve confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.
The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.
When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here’s that paper’s abstract:

items.excerpt:
New orders for metalworking machinery surpassed $1 billion in September as manufacturers continue investing to support growth.
Manufacturers and machine shops booked more than $1 billion in new orders for metalworking machinery in September, setting a record for monthly investment, according to the latest U.S. Manufacturing Technology Orders (USMTO) report , released Monday by AMT-The Association for Manufacturing Technology.
The USMTO report tracks new-order values and machine units for metal-cutting and metal-forming machinery nationwide and in six regions. The report serves as an economic indicator for future manufacturing activity, as companies invest to support expected production needs.
September’s numbers were boosted by orders placed during the International Machine Tool Show (IMTS), held September 11-14 in Chicago, and continued an upward trend in machinery investment. The totals marked the seventh straight month of orders exceeding half a billion dollars—the longest streak of investment in the report’s history, according to AMT.
September orders rose 38% compared to August and were up 101.7% from September 2025. The total value of orders placed in 2026 reached $5.76 billion through September—45% above the first three quarters of 2025.
September’s totals were 22.5% above the previous monthly record, set in December 2025 .
Orders accelerated across customer industries, including machine shops, aerospace manufacturing, and automotive manufacturing.
AMT calls for elevated activity for the remainer of 2026 and into 2027.
“The resilience of demand in the current expansion, which began in September 2024, can be attributed to the increased appetite for automation, demand from industries with long backlogs and lead times, and defense production, which should be sustained through any downturns in aggregate demand,” AMT researchers wrote. “Even if overall capital investment declines in the near future, the current level of demand for machined parts and heightened levels of capacity utilization could ensure that a good number of leads found at IMTS 2026 will convert into additional orders in the coming months.”

We’re enabling robots to learn faster for the real world - from everyday skills to the factory floor
Today, we are introducing Gemini Robotics 2.5, our most capable vision-language-action (VLA) model to date. Gemini Robotics 2.5 increases both the breadth of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it can acquire them. This enhances dexterity, reliability, and safety to help robots step out of the lab and into more unstructured, real-world environments, where they can assist people with a greater range of tasks.
Earlier this year, we brought whole-body intelligence to robots of many types, including humanoids. Now, in large part thanks to Gemini 4 Argon's ability to accelerate robotics research, we have further pushed the frontier of physical intelligence. Gemini Robotics 2.5 marks a leap forward in three key areas:
Gemini Robotics 2.5 is rolling out to our robotics partners .

With Gemini Robotics 2.5, we expanded the model capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity. items.excerpt:
High container volumes have led to backups at West Coast ports as cargo waits for rail cars.
Import volume at the nation’s major container ports is expected to taper off for the remainder of the year following an extended peak season that has kept docks busy since the spring, according to the Global Port Tracker report released today by the National Retail Federation (NRF) and Hackett Associates.
“U.S. ports have seen high volume levels throughout this year’s longer-than-usual peak season and numbers are still strong even as the season winds down,” NRF Vice President for Supply Chain and Customs Policy Jonathan Gold said. “Unfortunately, these volumes have led to backups at some ports, particularly on the West Coast where cargo has sat for extended periods waiting to be transferred to rail cars. We’ve also seen the threat of a strike at the nation’s largest port complex in recent days. Nonetheless, most holiday merchandise is already here, and retailers are working closely with their supply chain partners to ensure that the supply of holiday gifts continues to flow smoothly.”
A strike was avoided at the beginning of the month when International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26, which represents watchmen at a number of container terminals at the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, reached a short-term contract extension with the Pacific Maritime Association. The contract has now been extended three times for a few days at a time, most recently through Nov. 20, with no long-term agreement in place following the expiration of the previous contract in July 2025. Hackett Associates Founder Ben Hackett said this year’s months-long peak season was an offshoot of an extended season in 2025, when a series of tariff increases led retailers to bring in merchandise before the tariffs could take effect. “At the start of 2026, that surge appeared to have ended after the Supreme Court struck down high ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs. Expectations of another extended peak season consequently faded,” Hackett said. “However, new tariffs introduced in the second quarter prompted a renewed surge in imports beginning in May that continued through mid-October. items.excerpt:
Trucking conditions were weighed down by soaring diesel prices.
Business conditions in the trucking market eased slightly in September due to soaring diesel fuel prices, but remained solidly positive in the overall view, according to transportation analyst firm FTR.
The Bloomington, Indiana-based firm said its Trucking Conditions Index (TCI) declined modestly in September to 8.13 from August’s 11.5 reading due to record fuel costs and a pause in the trend toward stronger freight rates. However, FTR’s revised forecast calls for more favorable conditions for carriers over at least the next three quarters than in the prior outlook.
“Multiple signs point to a truck freight market that probably will be considerably stronger over the next few quarters than we had previously forecast,” Avery Vise, FTR’s vice president of trucking, said in a release. “Slow employment growth in trucking despite strong freight rates suggests head winds for adding drivers, including various enforcement initiatives. An increase in our freight volume forecast puts further upward pressure on capacity utilization.”
The TCI tracks the changes representing five major conditions in the U.S. truck market: freight volumes, freight rates, fleet capacity, fuel prices, and financing costs. Combined into a single index number, a positive score represents good, optimistic conditions. And conversely, a negative score represents bad, pessimistic conditions.

items.title: Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI
items.description: General, often expert, and sometimes jagged
items.excerpt:
Before getting started, I wanted to thank my readers for making my new book, Co-Existence, a New York Times bestseller two weeks in a row. If you haven’t read it, you can get a copy here .
I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch 1 , and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic’s newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I’ll go with: “an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer.” This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where “using a computer” is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers.
So as not to keep you in suspense, I think the answer is that this is “almost” AGI, or what I have called Jagged AGI. Even within my limited definition, there are still important areas in many tasks where AI is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability. But the jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations, which makes it harder to describe. So I want to try to do that in this post by showing you what Fable can do and where the gaps are. To get started I asked the new model: “I write OneUsefulThing among other stuff, I need you to create the most impressive thing I can share with people when you launch. It needs to be embeddable in a post and i can preface it however you like. it needs to have a visceral impact on people to show what you can do and the range of capabilities. It should grab them quickly. Be amazingly clever about this.”
Fable asked me not to reveal anything until you had watched its video to the end.
This was in one shot, with no feedback from me beyond the prompt. There is creativity here (including in the twist ending) and judgment and playfulness and cleverness. This is, I think, at the level of a human expert trying to make a movie with code alone, the sort of performance I would once have associated with AGI.

Handshake went from launch to $1B in one year pushing the envelope of specialized data for frontier labs. Our first deep dive into a data lab with specific examples across Finance, Bio, and Alignment
This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company . In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue . What are frontier labs buying at that scale? What evals are models still nowhere close to human level on? Garrett Lord brought the people who build these reinforcement learning environments to show us. For the first time, we are walking through them live!
To cover the scope of Handshake, we had to produce a very special joint podcast across our Science/Engineering/Research/Finance podcast hosts, because Handshake’s business runs across all these and more.
Watch for three segments after the general intro:
Finance. In the finance demo, the agent has to find its assignment in a bank’s email, work out which files govern the deal, and deliver a workbook. Watch what happens to one line in the client’s email about existing goodwill. The agent carries the number into Python and subtracts it. Collin points out that the model can explain the tax treatment when you ask it directly. The mistake comes when it has to recognize that this particular line of code is where the rule applies.
Bio. Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller show us VIALS, Handshake’s benchmark for interpreting the images scientists use at work. Nick puts nine slides of brain-tumor tissue on screen and asks which two show the most advanced vessel necrosis. Give yourself a moment before his answer. Nick picks H and I. The model picks those two and adds G. Watching Nick point to what’s missing from the tissue is more instructive than seeing the score.
Coding. In a simulated file-access task, the team can inspect which files an agent read, whether it checked the copies, and what it did to the shell history afterward. A transcript of the agent’s final reply would miss most of what Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka are evaluating.

items.excerpt:
As thieves increasingly target truckloads of high-value goods, industry experts urge shippers and carriers to strengthen their cyberdefenses.
Ben Ames has spent 30 years as a journalist since starting out as a reporter for daily newspapers in Pennsylvania and Massachusetts. He has focused on business and technology reporting since 1999 for trade journals including Cahners’ Design News and Modern Materials Handling magazines, and other magazines with PennWell and IDG. A native New Yorker, Ames went to college in Maine and now lives with his family outside of Boston, where they all love to hike and kayak.
Cargo theft is on the rise, and we’re not just talking about small-scale shoplifting. Across the globe, entire trailers and containers are going missing.
Newspaper headlines from the past year alone tell the story, describing how thieves swiped 11,000 bottles of bourbon from a North Philadelphia warehouse, $1.7 million worth of condoms headed to a Walmart DC in Pennsylvania, 40,000 pounds of Pabst Blue Ribbon beer from a California warehouse, $400,000 worth of lobsters from a Massachusetts seafood warehouse, and 400,000 KitKat chocolate bars from a warehouse in Poland.
But talk to the logistics professionals who oversee warehouse docks and freight yards, and few of them blame armed mobsters or masked carjackers. Rather, the culprits frequently drive up to a DC in broad daylight, present realistic-looking credentials, then hook up their tractor to a loaded trailer and cruise off down the highway. A few days later, that facility might get a call from a confused customer who never received their shipment. But by then it’s too late, and the entire load has vanished into thin air.
In the words of Curtis Spencer, CEO of global trade service specialist IMS Worldwide , “criminals are increasingly walking through the front door instead of breaking down a gate. Fictitious pickups, where someone shows up with forged carrier credentials and a booking that looks completely legitimate, are climbing fast, and [recent statistics show] that nearly a third of U.S. cargo theft incidents last year involved no forced entry at all: just a stolen identity, a cloned motor carrier number, or a hijacked email thread.”
LOWER VOLUME, HIGHER IMPACT So who’s to blame here? Industry experts say the answer is computer hackers, armed not with pistols and picklocks but with proficiency in the dark arts of spoofing, phishing, double brokering, and identity theft.

items.title: How to minimize Wi-Fi roaming interruptions for autonomous mobile robots
items.description: Dedicated Wi-Fi scan architectures can improve robot mobility, reliability, and performance, says Synaptics. The post How to minimize Wi-Fi roaming interruptions for autonomous mobile robots appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.excerpt:
Wi-Fi connectivity needs to be reliable for real-time mobile robot management. Source: Synaptics
An autonomous mobile robot or AMR may cross dozens of Wi-Fi coverage zones during a single shift. Each transition creates a small but potentially consequential communications problem: How does the robot find its next access point without interrupting the connection it is already using?
The answer matters because AMRs , industrial inspection robots, warehouse automation, and healthcare service robots increasingly depend on continuous connectivity for sensor data, telemetry, and control.
In a conventional Wi-Fi architecture, the primary communication radio must periodically stop transmitting and receiving application traffic while it searches for alternative access points. That creates a tradeoff among connectivity, latency, power consumption, and roaming performance.
A dedicated scan architecture separates network discovery from application traffic. The robot can monitor its wireless environment continuously while the primary radio maintains the active connection.
One implementation, Synaptics Scan Core, uses a low-power wireless subsystem to monitor neighboring access points while the primary Wi-Fi radio remains dedicated to application traffic. This separation can support faster roaming decisions, lower latency, reduced packet loss, and more efficient scanning.
Robots are becoming more connected and autonomous across manufacturing , logistics , healthcare , retail , and service environments. As they move through larger and more complex facilities, reliable wireless connectivity and fast roaming become core design requirements rather than secondary networking considerations.
Unlike stationary Wi-Fi devices, robots move continually between coverage areas while maintaining video, AI inference, telemetry, and fleet-management communications. These combined demands make mobile robotics a strong use case for dedicated scanning architectures.
Modern robots also support increasingly demanding wireless workloads, including HD and multi-camera video , simultaneous localization and mapping ( SLAM ), AI-assisted navigation , predictive maintenance, and remote operation.
Wireless connectivity has therefore evolved from a convenience into a critical operational subsystem.

items.title: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
items.excerpt:
A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions
In the financial sector, the utilization of real-world data faces significant constraints due to strict privacy regulations, compliance requirements, and the need for advanced domain expertise. In this context, the development of agentic AI in the financial domain requires synthetic data capable of avoiding the risks of using real data while reflecting demographics, household structures, and asset statuses to reproduce diverse, realistic financial scenarios.
To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan , a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset " Nemotron-Personas-Japan ." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs , a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer , an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).
This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development . The Nemotron-Personas collection , including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim , enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world.
It was built using NVIDIA’s framework for synthetic data generation, NeMo Data Designer . This compound AI system enables complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and support for multiple generation backends. items.title: America Can Build Again. Here’s How
items.description: Permitting Reform And The Race to Rebuild America
items.excerpt:
At the start of the Great Depression and with seemingly impossible engineering challenges before them, San Francisco began construction on the Golden Gate Bridge, a project long-derided as “the bridge that couldn’t be built.” Workers constructed what was then the world’s longest and tallest suspension bridge amid fierce currents, fog, and high winds. Construction began in January 1933. Cars crossed the bridge by May 1937. The cost was $35 million. The feat rivaled the construction of the Empire State Building a few years earlier: 102 stories in 410 days and a month ahead of schedule. It was an age of builders, where seemingly impossible feats of engineering, great and small, were routine across America.
Nearly a century later and five miles away, San Francisco commissioned another public work: the Noe Valley public toilet. The 150-square-foot bathroom containing one metal toilet and a baby changing station was projected to cost $1.7 million and take over two years to build. After public outcry, the city accepted a donated modular bathroom alongside pro bono engineering and architectural work. The project still cost taxpayers around $200,000, as the donated toilet still required permitting and sign off from over a half-dozen agencies, including the Arts Commission .
It is easy to handwave the Noe Valley toilet as an outlier, but the same sad tale repeats itself across the country:
California’s high-speed rail project has spent $13 billion of its original $33 billion budget with little to show for it. Its estimated total costs have ballooned to $128 billion.
In two decades, America has completed only two large nuclear reactors from the ground up, seven years late and roughly $23 billion over budget. At its peak, America completed four or five a year .
An Arizona mine capable of supplying a quarter of U.S. copper demand has sat idle since its 1995 discovery, facing a 35-plus-year path to production due to permitting and litigation.
A 550-mile transmission line took 17 years to complete. Construction took two years. Legal battles took the rest. Its sister project took 15 years.
A 94% complete West Virginia pipeline stood idle for nearly a decade amid permitting disputes resolved only by an act of Congress and Supreme Court order.

items.description: Two pallets arrive at a distribution center carrying the same product but different production lots and expiration dates. The warehouse management system (WMS) identifies the SKU, records the quantity, and directs putaway. If the lot attributes are not captured or maintained, the inventory looks interchangeable even though it is not. That difference becomes material when […] The post Sunrise 2027: The Barcode Can Carry the Data. Can the Supply Chain? appeared first on Logistics Viewpoints .
items.excerpt:
Two pallets arrive at a distribution center carrying the same product but different production lots and expiration dates. The warehouse management system (WMS) identifies the SKU, records the quantity, and directs putaway. If the lot attributes are not captured or maintained, the inventory looks interchangeable even though it is not. That difference becomes material when a recall or expiration-date exception forces the operation to establish exactly what moved, where, and to whom.
GS1’s Sunrise 2027 initiative makes this an opportune time to revisit a familiar problem. Two-dimensional (2D) barcodes can put more information on the product, but greater data capacity does not automatically translate into better operational control. The strategic issue is what happens to the information after the scan, as products cross packaging lines, receiving docks, inventory systems, and trading-partner boundaries.
Sunrise 2027 is an industry milestone aimed at enabling retail point-of-sale systems to read and process GS1-compliant 2D barcodes by the end of 2027. At a minimum, those systems need to extract the Global Trade Item Number (GTIN) for price lookup. It is not a requirement to retire UPC symbols in 2027, nor does it impose a corresponding scanning deadline on general warehousing or transportation operations. Linear and 2D codes will coexist during the transition.
There is a second distinction that tends to disappear in discussions of the new technology. Logistics organizations already use GS1-128 linear barcodes to encode lot numbers, dates, and other attributes, while Serial Shipping Container Codes (SSCCs) identify logistics units. Two-dimensional symbols, including GS1 DataMatrix and QR codes using GS1 Digital Link, offer greater capacity and different ways to connect physical products with digital information. They do not invent the concept of product traceability.
This evolution builds on a broader movement toward more connected product identification. As discussed in GS1’s New RFID Standard Makes Supply Chain Data Web-Native , the industry is increasingly concerned with linking physical identification to standardized information that enterprise applications can interpret and exchange. Barcode technology and RFID address different identification requirements, but both raise the same architectural question: how does information associated with a physical object become useful across multiple systems and organizations?

items.title: One in Six Supply Chain Leaders Report an AI Data Incident in Past Year
items.description: One in six leaders surveyed by InstaLILY reported an AI incident involving supplier or customer data, even as confidence in data controls remained high.
items.excerpt:
One in six leaders say an AI tool mishandled supplier or customer data at their company in the past year, according to new research from InstaLILY. That figure rose to 22% among supply chain respondents.
Most respondents (81%) reported no incident, while 3% were unsure. The research did not establish how serious the incidents were or whether data left the business.
The findings come from a Pollfish survey launched Oct. 9 of 250 managers and executives in supply chain, logistics, distribution, and wholesale whose companies use AI in daily work.
The findings show how far AI has reached into commercial data. Seventy-eight percent of respondents said their AI tools can access customer pricing and margins, and the same share said AI can reach customer purchase histories. Sixty-seven percent said their tools can access supplier pricing and rebate data.
Confidence is high anyway. Eighty-seven percent said they are very or somewhat confident their AI tools keep supplier and customer data separated, even though only 32% said that data sits in separate systems.
Customers and suppliers are paying attention. 63% said their company has been asked how it protects supplier or customer data. Of those, 47% said the question affected a decision about a vendor, software or AI tool.
The top barrier to keeping data separate was tools not built with that in mind (22%), followed closely by cost (21%) and a lack of technical expertise (20%). 90% said they would be more likely to choose AI built for distribution and supply chain over a general-purpose tool if it offered better control over that data. InstaLILY sells AI agents for distributors and logistics companies.
About half said their employer would bear the most responsibility for an exposure, compared with 23% who pointed to the AI vendor.

items.title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
items.excerpt:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.
Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization . Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.
Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance . Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.
Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.
In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers .

items.title: Logistics Index Is Highest in Two Years
items.description: Inventory levels picked up in October, at the fastest rate of expansion since September of 2022, according to Logistics Manager's Index..
items.excerpt:
Inventory levels are growing at a robust rate, according to the October Logistics Manager’s Index, which is at 70.7, up (+0.5) from September’s reading of 70.2.
This is the second-highest reading in four years, behind only June’s reading of 71.1.
Colorado State University, Florida Atlantic University, Rutgers University, and the University of Nevada, Reno, in conjunction with the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals (CSCMP), released the report on November 3.
The report offers the following analysis as excerpted below.
The index has now come in over 70.0 for three of the last five months; it had not cleared this threshold for over four years before this recent run.
This has been a year of expansion in the overall index, with average LMI readings coming in at 67.4. This is up significantly from 2025’s average of 58.7 and is the second-highest calendar-year average, behind only 2021, in the 10-year history of the index.
We also see significant expansion in Aggregate Logistics Costs in October, with the three cost/price metrics combining for a score of 257.5 (on a scale of 0-300), which is up (+11.4) from September’s reading of 246.1 this month.
This is the highest reading for this aggregate metric since March of 2022, when supply-driven inflation was rampant in the wake of both the cessation of COVID-era demand and the invasion of Ukraine. Given the pressure on logistics costs, it is likely that we will continue to see supply-driven inflation continue to increase in the near term.
No matter what happens with inflation in the future, it is clear that the inflation that has already occurred is impacting some consumers. The University of Michigan’s measure of U.S. consumer sentiment was down slightly (-0.1) to 48% in October.
This decline was driven almost entirely by buying conditions for durable goods, which were down 18% due to high interest rates and concerns regarding affordability. Consumer sentiment is down 15% since the start of the war with Iran and down 10% year-over-year – the “current economic conditions” metric is down 20% from October 2025.
Inventory Levels picked up in October, coming in notably higher (+8.0) at 66.9, which is their fastest rate of expansion since September of 2022. This was driven by movements in the second half of the month, when Inventory Levels expanded notably faster at 72.1 than the still fast – but more muted- rate of 61.8 in the first half of October.

items.excerpt:
Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work—I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today’s coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions.
The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That’s a lot of information to absorb.
It’s not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop!
It’s very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as “I’m not reading all of that”. It doesn’t matter how accurate or useful the information is, I’m instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me!
I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention.
I think I’ve found a low-effort way to do this that feels right.
The HTML elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this:
Crucially, is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow.
I’ve started using this for my AI-generated pull requests.
The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what’s going on—the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed.
I’ll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature.
The full agent-written essay then follows in a . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on—“Claude Opus 5.5 Medium” for example.
My PRs don’t feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details.
